think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 27-year-old Nepali male presents with acute high-grade fever, severe symmetric polyarthritis affecting small and large joints, enthesitis, tenosynovitis, marked leukocytosis (36,800/uL), ESR 87 mm/h, CRP 335 mg/L, and active glomerulonephritis with proteinuria and hematuria, preceded by 4 weeks of painful nodular and pigmentary skin lesions. The clinical presentation strikingly mimics severe autoimmune rheumatic disease (Adult-onset Still's disease, SLE with lupus nephritis, reactive arthritis, or systemic necrotizing vasculitis). The critical diagnostic clue is peripheral nerve enlargement (thickened ulnar nerves) pointing toward mycobacterial infection and Type 2 lepra reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum).
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs immediately after emergency room presentation, vital signs, physical examination (painful cutaneous nodules, pigmentary changes, polyarthritis, enthesitis, tenosynovitis, bilateral ulnar nerve thickening), and baseline laboratory investigations (WBC 36,800/uL, anemia, thrombocytosis, elevated ESR/CRP, azotemia, nephritic urinalysis with granular casts, negative ANA/RF/anti-CCP, normal plain radiographs of hands/feet), strictly prior to skin punch biopsy histopathology and initiation of multidrug antileprosy therapy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) or SLE / systemic vasculitis is ruled out by negative ANA, RF, anti-CCP, normal complement levels, and the presence of bilateral ulnar nerve thickening with skin biopsy demonstrating acid-fast bacilli in foamy macrophages. Reactive arthritis is ruled out by the absence of preceding enteric or genitourinary symptoms, normal joint radiographs, and bilateral peripheral nerve thickening.
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old male from Nepal presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, multiple joint pains, and joint swelling, preceded by a 4-week history of progressive, painful nodular skin lesions involving his face, scalp, bilateral ears, all four extremities, and upper chest. He reports severe pain in the small joints of both hands, bilateral elbows, knees, and feet. He denies headache, cough, abdominal pain, dysuria, diarrhea, or preceding respiratory or diarrheal illness, and reports no previous similar episodes.

On physical examination, he is febrile with an oral temperature of 38.0°C, pulse of 95 beats per minute, and blood pressure of 114/74 mmHg. Dermatologic examination reveals multiple tender, erythematous nodular skin lesions over his face, bilateral ears, and upper and lower extremities, alongside widespread hypopigmented and hyperpigmented macules; light touch and pinprick sensation over the cutaneous lesions is intact. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrates marked tenderness and swelling involving the bilateral metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, wrists, elbows, knees, and bilateral third and fourth metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. There is clinical evidence of enthesitis at the quadriceps tendon insertions on both knees, as well as bilateral wrist extensor tenosynovitis. Neurological examination reveals bilaterally thickened ulnar nerves without motor deficit or overt sensory neuropathy; cranial nerves are intact, and muscle strength is normal throughout. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are normal.

Laboratory evaluation reveals a marked leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 36,800 /uL (93% neutrophils), hemoglobin of 8.7 g/dL (MCV 74.6 fL, MCH 22.3 pg), and platelet count of 656,000 /uL. Blood urea nitrogen is 13.6 mmol/L (normal range, 2.5–6.7 mmol/L) and serum creatinine is 163 umol/L (normal range, 50.4–98.1 umol/L). Inflammatory markers are severely elevated, with a C-reactive protein of 335 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 87 mm/1h. Urinalysis demonstrates 2+ protein, 3+ erythrocytes, 103 WBCs/hpf, 486 RBCs/hpf, and granular casts; urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio is elevated at 117 mg/mmol (normal range, 0–45 mg/mmol). Serologic testing for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) is negative, and complement levels (C3, C4) are normal. Plain radiographs of the hands and feet demonstrate no erosions or joint space narrowing.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) or Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) / Systemic Vasculitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High-grade fever, symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, extreme leukocytosis (>35,000/uL), thrombocytosis, highly elevated acute-phase reactants (CRP 335 mg/L, ESR 87 mm/h), and active glomerulonephritis strongly mimic severe rheumatologic diseases such as AOSD or lupus nephritis. However, autoantibodies (ANA, RF, anti-CCP) were negative, complements were normal, and the patient exhibited bilaterally thickened ulnar nerve trunks alongside nodular lesions, pointing to a granulomatous mycobacterial infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Further investigation revealed negative ANA, RF, anti ccp and normal complements.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Reactive arthritis or Disseminated gonococcal infection
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute febrile polyarthritis accompanied by prominent lower-extremity enthesitis (quadriceps insertion) and wrist tenosynovitis is characteristic of reactive arthritis. However, there were no preceding gastrointestinal or genitourinary symptoms, plain radiographs of the hands and feet showed no periostitis or erosions, and reactive arthritis does not cause bilateral peripheral nerve enlargement.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There was no history of preceding diarrhea, upper respiratory tract infection or urinary tract infection.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when peripheral nerve enlargement in an endemic patient with tender nodules and polyarthritis led to a skin punch biopsy revealing non-necrotizing granulomas with foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli, confirming borderline tuberculoid leprosy presenting with erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 lepra reaction).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Skin biopsy revealed non-necrotizing granuloma with numerous foamy macrophages in dermis and subcutaneous fat. Small number of acid-fast bacilli was seen in some of the macrophages and biopsy result was reported as borderline tuberculoid. Leprosy was diagnosed on basis of typical skin lesion and skin biopsy finding.

editor_comments: Exemplary demonstration of lepra reaction mimicking acute rheumatologic disease. Strict breakpoint excluding biopsy histology and Fite-Faraco staining.
